{"blocks":[{"kind":"paragraph","markdown":"You already know that brewing is extraction, and that a cup can taste sour or bitter depending on how much is pulled out of the grounds. In this lesson you will learn the main dials you can turn to steer that extraction: **grind size** and **water temperature**. You will also learn how to taste your cup and decide what to change next.","citations":["{{frg_6}}","{{frg_13}}"],"objectiveIds":["{{id_10}}","{{id_12}}"]},{"kind":"paragraph","markdown":"### Grind size

Grinding exposes the inside of the bean to water. A finer grind has more surface area, so water extracts faster. A coarser grind extracts more slowly. Grind size also controls how fast water flows through a filter: fine grounds slow the flow and lengthen the contact time.","citations":["{{frg_6}}"],"objectiveIds":["{{id_10}}"]},{"kind":"table","markdown":"| Method | Grind size | Looks like |
|---|---|---|
| Espresso | Very fine | Flour |
| Pour-over (e.g. V60) | Medium-fine | Table salt |
| French press | Coarse | Sea salt |

A French press steeps coffee for about four minutes and uses a metal filter, so the grind must be coarse enough for the filter to hold the grounds back.","citations":["{{frg_7}}"],"objectiveIds":["{{id_10}}"]},{"kind":"callout","markdown":"**Why a burr grinder?** A burr grinder gives more even particles than a blade grinder, and even particles extract evenly.","citations":["{{frg_7}}"],"objectiveIds":["{{id_10}}"]},{"kind":"paragraph","markdown":"### Water temperature

Water between 90 and 96 °C extracts coffee well. **Light roasts** are dense and harder to extract, so water just off the boil, around 96 °C, suits them. **Dark roasts** extract easily and can taste harsh with very hot water, so 90 to 92 °C works better. Without a thermometer, let boiled water rest for about 30 seconds before pouring.","citations":["{{frg_8}}"],"objectiveIds":["{{id_11}}"]},{"kind":"paragraph","markdown":"### Taste, then adjust

Let the coffee cool a little before tasting, because flavours are easier to notice when the cup is warm rather than hot. Notice three things: acidity (bright, sour or flat), sweetness and bitterness, and body (how heavy the coffee feels in your mouth). Write down the recipe and what you taste so you can repeat a good cup.","citations":["{{frg_12}}"],"objectiveIds":["{{id_12}}"]},{"kind":"table","markdown":"| What you taste | Likely cause | One change to try |
|---|---|---|
| Sour and thin | Under-extraction | Grind finer, or use hotter water |
| Bitter and drying | Over-extraction | Grind coarser, or use cooler water |
| Balanced but too weak or too strong | Strength, not extraction | Change the ratio, not the grind |","citations":["{{frg_13}}"],"objectiveIds":["{{id_12}}"]},{"kind":"callout","markdown":"**Change one thing at a time.** Adjust grind size first when a cup tastes off: sour means grind finer, bitter means grind coarser. Changing just one variable lets you taste its effect.","citations":["{{frg_6}}","{{frg_13}}"],"objectiveIds":["{{id_12}}"]}]}
